description: Four golden signals (RED + Saturation) for a self-hosted Temporal Service, with SLO attainment and error budget burn on top.

links.title: Slow activities
links.tooltip: Activity spans over $trace_slow — dial the threshold in the header

links.title: Failed spans
links.tooltip: Errored spans. Empty on a healthy stack — `make chaos-failures` fills it

links.title: Service graph
links.tooltip: Who calls whom, with rate and latency per edge — built from spans, not config

links.title: All recent traces
links.tooltip: No filter. Start here when you do not yet know what you are looking for

links.title: CPU profiles
links.tooltip: Where the Worker's CPU went, by function. Continuous — no repro needed

panels.title: Service level — are we keeping the promise?
SLOs in breach
panels.description: Zero means every error budget still has room. Read this first; if it is zero the signals below are informational, not urgent.

panels.title: Error budget remaining
panels.description:
One tile per SLO. Saturates at -100%: past that the budget is gone and burn rate is the number that matters.

Read the value, not only the colour — green vs orange is near-indistinguishable under protanopia, so the signed percentage carries the meaning.

panels.title: Burn rate (1h)
panels.description:
Multiples of sustainable budget spend. 1x exhausts the budget exactly at the window's end; 14.4x is the fast-burn page threshold.

symlog axis: a real incident reaches 80x+, which on a linear axis flattens the 1x and 14.4x decision lines into the baseline.

panels.title: R — Rate  ·  how much work is arriving
Cluster request rate
panels.description: All Frontend gRPC calls, long-polls included — this is traffic, and a Worker polling IS traffic. A sudden drop here with no error rise usually means callers stopped, not that you broke.

panels.title: Frontend request rate by operation
panels.description: Top 6 operations. PollWorkflowTaskQueue and PollActivityTaskQueue normally dominate — that is Workers waiting for work, not load. Watch the shape of StartWorkflowExecution for real demand.

panels.title: Workflow throughput
panels.description: Started vs completed. A persistent gap means work is accumulating — the single clearest early sign of a saturated Worker fleet, and it shows up here long before anything errors.

panels.title: E — Errors  ·  what is failing, and whose fault is it
Frontend error ratio
panels.description: Server-fault ratio. Client-caused errors (Canceled, NotFound, InvalidArgument) are excluded — counting them measures your callers' behaviour, not your availability.

panels.title: Server-fault rate by type
panels.description: Faults that are yours. ResourceExhausted points at rate limiting or datastore pressure; Internal/Unavailable points at cluster health. Empty here on a healthy cluster is correct, not broken.

panels.title: Workflow outcomes
panels.description:
The application signal, not the cluster signal. Activity failures absorbed by retries are HEALTHY and do not appear here.

Watch timeout specifically: a saturated fleet produces timeouts, not failures. Measured under a backlog storm, failed sat at 0.02/s while timeout hit 24.6/s.

panels.title: D — Duration  ·  how long it takes
Frontend latency (long-polls excluded)
panels.description: Long-poll operations are EXCLUDED. They block up to 60s by design and are the highest-volume Frontend calls; including them makes this panel measure Worker idle time. Measured: 95.9% under 500ms with polls in, 100% with them out.

panels.title: Persistence P95 by operation
panels.description: Check this BEFORE scaling any Temporal service. The datastore is upstream of nearly every Temporal latency symptom — most self-hosted incidents are persistence incidents wearing a different hat.

panels.title: Schedule-to-start P99
panels.description:
Queue wait, not execution time — how long work sat before a Worker picked it up. The customer-visible symptom of an undersized fleet.

If this is flat during a known backlog, ScheduleToStartTimeout is set in Activity Options and is truncating the metric.

panels.title: S — Saturation  ·  how close to the limit
Worker slot utilisation

targets.expr:
sum by (task_queue) (temporal_worker_task_slots_used{namespace!~"temporal_system|system|_unknown_"})
/ clamp_min(
    sum by (task_queue) (temporal_worker_task_slots_used{namespace!~"temporal_system|system|_unknown_"})
  + sum by (task_queue) (temporal_worker_task_slots_available{namespace!~"temporal_system|system|_unknown_"}), 1)

panels.description:
Fraction of Worker capacity in use. At 100% with LOW host CPU, raise MaxConcurrentActivityExecutionSize — do not add Workers. At 100% with HIGH host CPU, add Workers.

That discriminator is host CPU, which is NOT a Temporal metric: you need node_exporter or cAdvisor alongside this or the two cases are indistinguishable.

panels.title: Sync match rate
panels.description:
Share of Tasks handed straight to a waiting Worker instead of being written to the datastore first. High is good and cheap; a fall means Workers were not ready when work arrived.

Near-zero on an IDLE queue is meaningless, not bad — the ratio needs real poll traffic to mean anything.

panels.title: Tasks with no poller
panels.description:
Work queued for a Task Queue nobody is polling. The one signal here with no false-positive mode — anything above zero is real.

Usually a Task Queue name mismatch or a Worker fleet that is entirely down. Nothing fails; the work just never runs. Scaling Workers will not fix a name mismatch.

panels.title: K — Worker cache  ·  watch, do not page
Sticky cache size vs forced evictions
panels.description:
WATCH tier, not an alert.

Sticky cache size approaching WorkflowCacheSize drives forced evictions, and every eviction means the next Workflow Task replays the whole history instead of resuming from cache. That shows up as workflow task execution latency, not as an error — which is why it is worth plotting before it becomes a latency incident.

TWO SCALES, TWO AXES. Cache size is a GAUGE (a count of cached executions); evictions are a RATE (per second). On a shared axis the eviction rate is invisible whenever the cache is non-trivially sized — which is exactly when you need to see it. Evictions are on the right axis, in red.

A flat non-zero cache with zero evictions is the healthy state.

panels.title: L — Logs  ·  the only place an execution ID may live
Log volume by service and level
panels.description:
Error and warning lines per second, from Loki.

Level is extracted with an ANCHORED regex on the line prefix. An unanchored match tags any line containing the word 'error' — which produced 644 phantom worker errors before it was fixed.

panels.title: Temporal Service errors (infra)
panels.description: Server-side errors and warnings, JSON-parsed. This is where a persistence error or a shard problem explains a metric spike that the dashboards above can only show you the shape of.

panels.title: Find stuck executions (workflow IDs)
panels.description:
THE PANEL METRICS CANNOT REPLACE.

Surfaces worker log lines for non-determinism and Workflow Task failures, which carry WorkflowID and RunID.

TMPRL1100 = non-determinism; TMPRL1101 = deadlock detected during workflow run (a Workflow Task taking too long, usually a blocking call in Workflow code). Both codes verified present in this stack by forcing a real NDE with `make chaos-nde`. The Loki datasource defines derived fields on both, so each ID is a link straight into the Temporal UI.

On servers below 1.30 (no TemporalReportedProblems) this is the primary route from a stuck-workflow alert to the affected executions.

panels.title: M — Workflow duration SLO  ·  the executions nothing else can see
Duration compliance
panels.description:
Closed-in-budget / (closed-in-budget + closed-over-budget + still running past 1x budget).

The third term is why terminating a stuck Workflow does NOT improve this number: the execution moves from that term to closed-over-budget and the ratio is unchanged. Verified end to end — 5 executions moved and compliance held at 0.793336 exactly.

panels.title: Open executions past budget
panels.description:
OPEN executions that have exceeded N x their duration budget.

No alert above this row can see these. They are Running, pollers are healthy, nothing has failed and nothing is retrying — only duration is wrong, and no Prometheus counter carries duration for an open execution.

Measured during `make chaos-stuck`: 0 -> 5 at buckets 1 and 2 while no other alert fired.

panels.title: Running executions
panels.description: Open executions by type. Deliberately NOT alertable on its own: this number scales with business volume, not with health. It is here as the denominator context for the panel to its left.

panels.title: Poll freshness
panels.description:
Age of the newest successful Visibility poll.

THIS PANEL GUARDS THE ROW. The monitor never publishes a zero when a query fails — it leaves the previous value in place, because a 0 would read as 'nothing is over budget' during exactly the outage when that is least likely to be true. The cost is that a frozen gauge looks perfectly healthy, and this is the only thing that reveals it.

panels.title: Server-reported stuck detection
panels.description:
1 = TemporalReportedProblems works here. 0 = it does not, so stuck_executions is NOT PUBLISHED AT ALL.

Absence rather than zero is deliberate: a stuck_executions gauge sitting at 0 on a server without the attribute is indistinguishable from a clean bill of health. Needs Server 1.30+ and, self-hosted, system.numConsecutiveWorkflowTaskProblemsToTriggerSearchAttribute — so on 1.27.4 this correctly reads 0.

Duration buckets (left) work on every version and remain the primary signal.

panels.title: N — Traces & profiles  ·  where the time actually went
Open in Explore — the query is already written
panels.description:
Each button opens Explore on a pre-filled query, over the time range this dashboard is currently showing.

The panels below are span METRICS — aggregates derived from sampled traces. They tell you a CLASS of work got slower. Only a trace tells you which execution, and where inside it the time went. These buttons are the shortest path from one to the other.

TWO THINGS THAT LOOK LIKE BREAKAGE AND ARE NOT:

- An activity span times EXECUTION, not the queue wait before a Worker picked the task up. That wait is schedule-to-start, in rows D and S. During `make chaos-backlog` the fleet can be minutes behind while every activity span stays a few milliseconds, so 'Slow activities' correctly stays empty.

- 'Failed spans' is empty whenever nothing has failed. `make chaos-failures` populates it.

If EVERY button lands on the Grafana home page instead of Explore, the viewer lacks the datasources:explore permission — see GF_USERS_VIEWERS_CAN_EDIT in docker-compose.yml.

panels.title: Span latency p95 by operation (from traces)
panels.description:
p95 per span, derived from sampled traces by Tempo's metrics generator.

ESTIMATE, not an SLI — sampling makes it approximate, and the SDK histograms above are exact. Its value is the breakdown: this tells you WHICH activity is slow, which no SDK metric does.

Click any series to open the slow traces behind it.

panels.title: Span throughput by operation
panels.description:
Calls per second per span. Useful for spotting an Activity being retried far more often than its siblings — a retry storm shows here as throughput without matching Workflow completions.

Click any series to open that span's traces.

panels.title: P — Poll outcomes  ·  is the fleet the right SIZE?
Poll Outcome Mix
panels.description:
EVERY POLL ENDS IN EXACTLY ONE OF THESE THREE, so the stack is the complete picture of what your pollers are doing.

  sync match  — a Worker was waiting; the Task went straight to it. Best case.
  async match — the Task was delivered, but had to be PERSISTED first because no Worker was ready. Growing band = starvation.
  empty       — the poll waited its full 60s and found nothing. Growing band = over-provisioning.

ASYNC MATCH IS A SUBTRACTION, NOT A COUNTER. Temporal exposes no async-match metric; it is poll_success - poll_success_sync, clamped at zero for the scrape skew where the two counters land in different windows.

poll_timeouts is NOT async match. It counts polls that found NOTHING. Reading it as async match inverts the conclusion entirely — a flooded fleet would read as a starved one.

Scenario 1 (backlog) and 4 (slots) grow the ASYNC band.
Scenario 8 (poller flood) grows the EMPTY band.

panels.title: Sync Match Rate vs Poll Success Rate
panels.description:
TWO RATIOS THAT LOOK ALIKE AND MEASURE UNRELATED THINGS. They are on one axis deliberately, because the whole lesson is that they diverge.

SYNC MATCH RATE — sync / all delivered. 'Was a Worker waiting?' A HEALTH signal. It has no benign low state, which is why TemporalSyncMatchRateLow needs no second condition (only a volume guard for the idle case).

POLL SUCCESS RATE — matched / (matched + empty). 'Did polls find work?' A SIZING signal. It has TWO opposite low states:
  low + schedule-to-start HIGH → starved. Add Workers.
  low + schedule-to-start ~0   → flooded. REMOVE Workers.

That ambiguity is why nothing pages on this alone. TemporalMatchingStarved requires schedule-to-start as a second condition; the over-provisioned case is TemporalWorkerFleetOverProvisioned at severity INFO, because it is a cost finding rather than an incident.

During `make chaos-poller-flood`, poll success rate collapses and sync match rate does NOT move. That divergence is the finding.

panels.title: Discriminator — schedule-to-start P99 and free slots
panels.description:
THE TWO READINGS THAT SETTLE STARVED vs OVER-PROVISIONED IN ONE GLANCE, when poll success rate has already told you something is off but not which direction.

  s2s CLIMBING + slots at ZERO  → starved. Tasks are waiting. Scenarios 1 and 4.
  s2s ~0 + slots FREE           → NOT starved. Nothing is waiting; the low poll success rate is idle pollers. Scenario 8.

Two axes and two units on purpose: seconds on the left, a count on the right. Sharing an axis would squash schedule-to-start flat against a slot count in the thousands, which is exactly when you need to read it.

UNITS: seconds, because this stack is the Go SDK. On a Core-based SDK (TypeScript, Python, .NET) the same series name carries MILLISECONDS and the 0.2 threshold is wrong by 1000x. Run `make verify-sdk-labels`.

Scenarios 1 and 4 look IDENTICAL on this panel. Host CPU is what separates them, and it is not a Temporal metric — use `docker stats` or node_exporter.

panels.title: Which shape am I looking at?
panels.description: The scenario matrix, on the board rather than in the runbook. Scenario 8 is the only row where poll success rate is the ONLY thing that moved.

options.content:
| | Sync match | Poll success | S2S P99 | Slots | Host CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Healthy | ~100% | high | ~0 | free | moderate |
| Backlog **(1)** | ↓ | high | ↑ | 0 | **high** |
| Slot starve **(4)** | ↓ | high | ↑ | 0 | **low** |
| **Poller flood (8)** | **~100%** | **↓↓** | **~0** | **free** | low |
| Blackout **(5)** | ↓↓ | — | blank | blank | — |

**Scenario 8 is the only row where poll success rate is the only thing that moved.** A starved fleet and a flooded fleet both push it down and need *opposite* responses.

**Host CPU is not a Temporal metric.** It comes from `docker stats` or node_exporter. Without it, scenarios 1 and 4 are indistinguishable here — same reason the runbook insists on node-level metrics in the same Grafana.

Blackout shows *blank*, not zero: SDK metrics come from the Workers, so an absent Worker emits nothing at all.
